OFA-Diffusion Compression: Compressing Diffusion Model in One-Shot Manner

DOI: XXXXXXX.XXXXXXXConference: The 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia; November 10–14, 2026; Rio de Janeiro, BrazilISBN: 978-1-4503-XXXX-X/2026/11

Affiliation: Renmin University of China, Beijing, China email: jianghaoyang233@ruc.edu.cn , Zekun Wang Affiliation: Alibaba Inc., Hangzhou, China email: zkwang@ir.hit.edu.cn , Mingyang Yi Note: Corresponding author. Abstract.

The Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DPM) achieves remarkable performance in image generation, while its increasing parameter size and computational overhead hinder its deployment in practical applications. To improve this, the existing literature focuses on obtaining a smaller model with a fixed architecture through model compression. However, in practice, DPMs usually need to be deployed on various devices with different resource constraints, which leads to multiple compression processes, incurring significant overhead for repeated training. To obviate this, we propose a once-for-all (OFA) compression framework for DPMs that yields different subnetworks with various computations in a one-shot training manner. The existing OFA framework typically involves massive subnetworks with different parameter sizes, while such a huge candidate space slows the optimization. Thus, we propose to restrict the candidate subnetworks with a certain set of parameter sizes, where each size corresponds to a specific subnetwork. Specifically, to construct each subnetwork with a given size, we gradually allocate the maintained channels by their importance. Furthermore, we propose a reweighting strategy to balance the optimization process of different subnetworks. Experimental results show that our approach can produce compressed DPMs for various sizes with significantly lower training overhead while achieving satisfactory performance. The code is available at https://github.com/atrijhy/OFA-Diffusion_Compression.

Keywords: 
Diffusion Models, Model Compression, U-Net, Vision Transformer, Once-for-all Compression

1. Introduction

Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021b) have attracted great attention in image synthesis due to their stable training paradigm and heightened controllability (Ramesh et al., 2022; Rombach et al., 2022). Despite the superior performance of DPM, its inference process usually requires excessive computational overhead, due to the necessity of computing through complex architectures with numerous parameters (typical U-Nets (Ronneberger et al., 2015), DiT (Peebles and Xie, 2023), and U-ViT (Bao et al., 2023)) over multiple denoising steps. The massive inference cost hinders the deployment of DPMs on devices under specific efficiency constraints (Chen et al., 2023).

To mitigate this, the existing literature proposes to reduce the denoising steps by properly designed numerical samplers (Song et al., 2021a; Lu et al., 2022; Salimans and Ho, 2022; Meng et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Xue et al., 2023; Yi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Yi et al., 2023). Although these methods significantly reduce denoising steps, the volume of model parameters remains an efficiency bottleneck for each denoising step. Specifically, on edge devices, even a minimal number of evaluation steps can be slow or impractical. Therefore, compressing the architecture of DPMs, e.g., by pruning (Li et al., 2023b; Fang et al., 2023), knowledge distillation (Kim et al., 2023), or quantization (Li et al., 2023a; He et al., 2023a) has become more crucial. Nevertheless, the aforementioned compression methods compress the original DPM to a fixed size, while the resource constraints (e.g., parameter size, power, latency) vary widely in real-world deployment scenarios. Thus, deploying a single fixed model across all types of devices is not feasible. Moreover, compressing specialized DPMs for each device requires multiple compression and retraining processes, which is computationally expensive and uneconomical. Thus, to amortize the expensive multiple compression overhead, it is desirable to compress DPMs into different sizes in a one-shot manner.

To this end, we propose a once-for-all (OFA) Diffusion Compression framework: jointly compresses different subnetworks in a one-shot training manner and adapts the computation flexibly by selecting the channel widths11 1 Refers to the number of channels in layers.. Thus, the OFA compression not only significantly enriches the number of architectural configurations for deployment (more than dozens in our work), but also reduces the training overhead of subnetworks. Notably, OFA training has been proposed for classification networks or GAN networks. In existing methods, for each update step, the update direction can be obtained by enumerating all subnetworks (Yu and Huang, 2019; Hou et al., 2020; Hou et al., 2021) or sample a random architectural configuration (Fan et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021). However, neither is appropriate in our setting: The former method is computationally impractical when scaling to our intended scales of subnetworks (more than dozens). The latter method has a huge candidate space, while we focus only on subnetworks that are at the Pareto frontier of performance and resource budgets in real-life deployment (Pan et al., 2023), thus massive useless candidates are ignored. Moreover, the huge space hinders the convergence of OFA training and requires an additional post-training search process. Thus, to improve OFA training for DPMs, we propose to specify the subnetwork for each size.

However, unifying the training process of different subnetworks with shared parameters is non-trivial, as the optimization of these subnetworks can negatively interfere with each other, leading to a slow convergence. Thus, the core problem becomes how to wisely construct the candidate subnetworks. To mitigate negative interference and meanwhile fully utilize the information adopted from pre-trained DPM, we propose to keep more important channels to be shared across more subnetworks. Specifically, we first calculate the channel sensitivity criterion (Molchanov et al., 2017) as its importance score. Then, for each target parameter size in training, we propose to prune channels in the same layer by ascending order of their importance scores, until the desired budget is attained. Taking into account the different importance of layers in DPM (Kim et al., 2023), we also introduce a strategy to maintain more parameters in more important layers. After obtaining the desired candidate subnetworks, we simultaneously train them in a one-shot manner. Moreover, considering the subnetworks of different sizes have different convergence rates during training, we propose a reweighting training strategy to balance the convergence of their optimization. Experimental results on various datasets show that our OFA diffusion compression framework only needs to be trained once while producing subnetworks with similar or even better performance compared to separately compressed models across various parameter sizes.

2. Related Work

Model Compression of DPMs.

Model compression aims to reduce the redundant parameters of large models and save the practical computations (Han et al., 2016), including pruning (LeCun et al., 1989; Hassibi et al., 1993; Han et al., 2015), knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Romero et al., 2015), or quantization (Rastegari et al., 2016; Hou et al., 2017) techniques. Considering the large computational overhead of DPM (Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2021b), it is natural to apply these techniques to it. (Kim et al., 2023) drops redundant layer and utilizes knowledge distillation to mimic the original DPM. (Fang et al., 2023) prunes unimportant channels based on training loss. (Li et al., 2023b) performs an evolutionary search to identify redundant blocks and then prunes the model until it satisfies the desired budget. Leveraging quantization technique to accelerate DPMs has also been explored (Shang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023a; He et al., 2023a; He et al., 2023b). Although these works make great progress in compressing DPMs, the resulting single fixed model is not suitable for all deployment scenarios, as we have mentioned in Section 1. Thus, we focus on compressing a pre-trained DPM into a range of smaller models with varied budgets (parameter sizes or latency) in a one-shot manner, which is critical in practice but remains unexplored.

Once-for-All (OFA) Training

To alleviate the excessive overhead of retraining from scratch for different models, the once-for-all framework aims to train a single network that supports diverse architectural settings and selects only a part of the OFA network in inference based on device requirements (Cai et al., 2020). Slimmable network (Yu et al., 2019; Yu and Huang, 2019) is a typical OFA model that adjusts the network width configuration, permitting instant and adaptive performance-efficiency trade-offs at run-time. (Lin et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2021) extend this method to GANs for generative tasks. On the other hand, (Hou et al., 2020) compresses BERT (Devlin et al., 2019) into smaller models with adaptive width and depth at once, and finally deploys them in various scenarios. In this work, we generalize such OFA compression technique to DPM. Notably, (Liu et al., 2023) independently train several DPMs of different sizes from scratch, applying proper structures during different steps of sampling process. The idea is similar to OFA compression, while their method is not scalable with the number of architectures. This is because the computational cost of training their DPMs are linearly increased with the number of candidate models. However, the subnetworks in our OFA compression framework are adopted from the same model, thus obviate the limitations in computational cost (Liu et al., 2023).

3. Preliminaries

Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs).

DPMs (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015; Ho et al., 2020) are generative models that gradually introduce Gaussian noise to real data through a forward diffusion process and generate samples via a backward denoising process. Following (Song et al., 2021b), we introduce DPMs in a continuous-time manner. Generally, in the forward process, the noisy data distribution pt​(𝒙)p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x}) is diffused from the real data 𝒙0∼pdata​(𝒙)\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\sim p_{\text{data}}(\boldsymbol{x}), through a stochastic differential equation (SDE) (Oksendal, 2013):

(1) d​𝒙t=𝝁⁡(xt,t)​d​t+σ⁡(t)​d​𝒘t,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}_{t}=\text{\boldmath{$\mu$}}(x_{t},t)\mathrm{d}t+\sigma(t)\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{w}_{t},

where 𝝁\mu and σ\sigma denote the drift and diffusion coefficients respectively, 𝒘t\boldsymbol{w}_{t} is the standard Wiener process. For a large TT, we can get 𝒙T≈𝒩⁡(0,𝑰)\boldsymbol{x}_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{I}). Then, by running the following reverse time probability flow ordinary differential equation

(2) d𝒙t=[𝝁(xt,t)−12σ(t)2∇logpt(𝒙t)]dt,\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{x}_{t}=\left[\text{\boldmath{$\mu$}}(x_{t},t)-\frac{1}{2}\sigma(t)^{2}\nabla\log p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t})\right]\mathrm{d}t,

started from 𝒙T≈𝒩⁡(0,𝑰)\boldsymbol{x}_{T}\approx\mathcal{N}(0,\boldsymbol{I}) (𝒙T\boldsymbol{x}_{T} is standard Gaussian in practice), we can sample 𝒙0∼pdata​(𝒙)\boldsymbol{x}_{0}\sim p_{\rm data}(\boldsymbol{x}).

In this paper, we use the formulation of EDM (Karras et al., 2022), such that 𝝁⁡(xt,t)=𝟎\text{\boldmath{$\mu$}}(x_{t},t)=\mathbf{0} and σ⁡(t)=2​t\sigma(t)=\sqrt{2t} with σ⁡(t)∈[0.002,80]\sigma(t)\in\left[0.002,80\right]. A neural network 𝒔𝜽​(𝒙t,t)\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t), is optimized to approximate the score function by minimizing the score matching loss (Song and Ermon, 2019):

(3) ℒ𝜽=𝔼t{λ(t)𝔼𝒙t[∥𝒔𝜽(𝒙t,t)−∇𝒙tlogp0​t(𝒙t|𝒙0)∥22]},\mathcal{L}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\!\!=\!\!{\mathbb{E}}_{t}\Bigl\{\lambda(t){\mathbb{E}}_{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}\bigl[\bigl\|\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t)-\nabla_{\boldsymbol{x}_{t}}\log p_{0t}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}|\boldsymbol{x}_{0})\bigl\|_{2}^{2}\bigl]\Bigl\},

where λ⁡(t)\lambda(t) controls the importance weight of different time steps. During sampling, the output of neural network 𝒔𝜽​(𝒙t,t)\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t},t) replaces ∇log⁡pt​(𝒙t)\nabla\log p_{t}(\boldsymbol{x}_{t}) in (2). The obtained samples 𝒙^0\hat{\boldsymbol{x}}_{0} can be viewed as an approximation to data from pdata​(𝒙)p_{\text{data}}(\boldsymbol{x}).

U-Net Architecture

Generally, the U-Net (Ronneberger et al., 2015) is the primary architecture (i.e., 𝒔𝜽\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} in (3)) in DPMs (Ho et al., 2020; Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021; Rombach et al., 2022). The U-Net consists of nn pairs of downsampling-upsampling blocks {Di,Ui}i=1n\{D_{i},U_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}, and another middle block MM, where ii are distinguished by the resolution of the block. At the end of DiD_{i} (resp. UiU_{i}), a downsample (resp. upsample) convolution is inserted to reduce (resp. recover) the resolution of feature maps. For each pair of blocks, there exist skip connections from DiD_{i} to UiU_{i} to transfer low-level information (see Appendix A for a detailed illustration of the U-Net architecture). In each layer of block (DiD_{i}, UiU_{i} or MM), there exist several stacked 3×33\times 3 convolution modules (C​o​n​v1Conv_{1} and C​o​n​v2Conv_{2}), followed by group normalization (Wu and He, 2018). These components consist of a ResNet layer (He et al., 2016). Besides that, some of these layers are followed by a spatial self-attention module (Vaswani et al., 2017; Salimans et al., 2017).

Vision Transformer

As an alternative to U-Net, Vision Transformer (ViT) based architectures (Peebles and Xie, 2023; Bao et al., 2023) replace the convolution layers with a pure transformer backbone as the score network 𝒔𝜽\boldsymbol{s}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}. Concretely, for ViT-based architectures, the input image with resolution H×WH\times W is firstly patchified into a sequence of N=H​Wp2N=\frac{HW}{p^{2}} tokens with patch size pp. These tokens are then processed by a stack of LL transformer blocks {Tl}l=1L\{T_{l}\}_{l=1}^{L}. Each block TlT_{l} consists of a multi-head self-attention (MSA) module (Vaswani et al., 2017) and a position-wise feed-forward network (FFN). Unlike traditional convolution neural networks, transformer backbones apply global self-attention across all tokens at every layer to capture long-range dependencies. In this work, we adopt U-ViT (Bao et al., 2023) as the representative ViT-based backbone for DPMs. As shown in the left part of Figure 1, U-ViT further introduces long skip connections between shallow blocks TlT_{l} and deep blocks TL−l+1T_{L-l+1}, similar in spirit to the {Di,Ui}\{D_{i},U_{i}\} skip connections in U-Net, to better capture low-level representations.

4. Constructing Subnetworks Set

In this section, we present details of the construction of subnetworks in our OFA-Diffusion Compression framework. The overview of the framework is shown in Figure 1.

In previous OFA work (Yu et al., 2019; Cai et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020), the subnetworks are randomly constructed at each update step. However, they produce massive subnetworks whose update direction can interfere with each other, slowing down the convergence of training and causing significant performance degradation on DPMs (see Figure 3) compared to subnetworks trained independently.

To accelerate the convergence of OFA training, we propose to reduce the number of candidate subnetworks (e.g., from thousands to dozens). It is worth noting that dozens of subnetworks in different sizes are enough to meet the practical deployment, since the deployment dedicate to find the subnetworks on the Pareto frontier of performance and resource budgets (Pan et al., 2023), so that many useless subnetworks are ignored. Concretely, we specify a list of parameter retention rates (consisting of dozens of candidates): {𝒫i}i=1N\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, with 𝒫1<⋯<𝒫N\mathcal{P}_{1}<\cdots<\mathcal{P}_{N}, and each 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} corresponds to a specific constructed subnetwork. Next, we describe the details of constructing these subnetworks.

4.1. Estimation of Channel Importance

In practice, compressing the DPMs either removes entire layers  (Kim et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b) or prune channels of features to reduce the width of model (Fang et al., 2023). However, removing coarse-grained units such as layers, usually leads to a significant performance drop (Xia et al., 2022). Therefore, we focus on reducing the width of layers by pruning channels. Concretely, for each removed channel of features, the weights of compressed modules (convolutions and self-attention as in Figure 1) connected to this channel will be eliminated following previous work (Fang et al., 2023). To obtain subnetwork with retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, for all blocks, we set their retention rates uniformly as 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} 22 2 A model with retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} can have different retention rates across blocks. However, we find that varying retention rates over blocks does not bring extra benefits. Thus, retention rates are invariant across blocks.. By doing this, we can directly control the actual computation overhead (e.g., MACs) with the retention rates of subnetworks.

Then, we describe how to construct subnetworks with different channel widths. Since subnetworks are trained jointly by sharing weights, it is intuitive to suggest that more important channels should be shared by more subnetworks to reduce interference between them. To do this, we first estimate the importance of channels. As channel contributions to model performance have been observed to vary in the same layer (He et al., 2017), we use the sensitivity criterion (Molchanov et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022) to measure the importance of channels, as in (Fang et al., 2023). The criterion is obtained by the variation of training loss (3) when the target channel is removed. Intuitively, the channel is considered important when this removal elicits a significant influence on the loss. Specifically, for the weight of the ii-th channel 𝒄i\boldsymbol{c}_{i}, its importance IicI_{i}^{c} is approximated by the first-order Taylor expansion of ℒ\mathcal{L} on 𝒄i=𝟎\boldsymbol{c}_{i}=\mathbf{0}:

(4) IiC=|ℒ−ℒ𝒄i=𝟎|=|(𝒄i−𝟎)⊤∇ℒ+R𝒄i=𝟎)|\displaystyle I_{i}^{C}=\left|\mathcal{L}-\mathcal{L}_{\boldsymbol{c}_{i}=\mathbf{0}}\right|=\left|(\boldsymbol{c}_{i}-\mathbf{0})^{\top}\nabla\mathcal{L}+R_{\boldsymbol{c}_{i}=\mathbf{0}})\right| ≈|𝒄i⊤∇ℒ|,\displaystyle\approx\left|\boldsymbol{c}_{i}^{\top}\nabla\mathcal{L}\right|,

where R𝒄i=𝟎R_{\boldsymbol{c}_{i}=\mathbf{0}} denotes the high-order remainder. In practice, we approximate ICI^{C} in (4) with its empirical mean.

4.2. Greedy Strategy for Channel Allocation among Layers

In the above section, we describe how to estimate the channel importance. In practice, the subnetwork architecture is obtained after specifying the number of channels maintained in each layer. Since the retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} is invariant between blocks as mentioned before, our goal in the sequel is to specify the channel allocation in each layer of blocks.

In the existing literature (Yu et al., 2019; Hou et al., 2020; Hou et al., 2021) the retention rates are also invariant among layers. However, the importance of layers in the same block varies significantly in DPMs (Kim et al., 2023) (Figure 8 in Appendix), which may cause the invariant strategy to be suboptimal for channel allocation. Therefore, we propose a greedy strategy that flexibly allocates the number of channels among layers based on layer importance scores.

To do this, for the layer ll of a block with KK layers in total, we calculate its importance score IlLI^{L}_{l}, by aggregating the importance of all channels in it: IlL=∑𝒄i∈lI𝒄icI^{L}_{l}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{c}_{i}\in l}I_{\boldsymbol{c}_{i}}^{c}. We observe that the layer importance ILI^{L} generally match the performance drop of eliminating layers (see Appendix D). With these importance scores of the layers, we proceed to allocate the channels maintained in each layer. As the retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} is invariant across blocks, the number of channels maintained in each block is K​𝒫i​|l|K\mathcal{P}_{i}|l|, where |l||l| is the original number of channels in each layer of block. Based on IlLI_{l}^{L}, we propose to maintain

(5) Cl=max⁡{min⁡{⌈IlL∑lIlL​K​𝒫i​|l|⌉,|l|},⌈𝒫0​|l|⌉}C_{l}=\max\left\{\min\left\{\left\lceil\frac{I_{l}^{L}}{\sum_{l}I_{l}^{L}}K\mathcal{P}_{i}|l|\right\rceil,|l|\right\},\lceil\mathcal{P}_{0}|l|\rceil\right\}

channels in layer ll, where the min\min and max\max operations are respectively to guarantee the upper and lower bounds (the lower bound guarantees no layers are entirely removed) of maintained channels in compressed layers. After that, the retention rate for each module in this layer is set as |Cl|/|l||C_{l}|/|l|.33 3 Theoretically, the retention rates of modules in a layer can be varied. However, we find that keeping them invariant is more computational efficient in practice. Notably, due to (5), the resulted subnetwork corresponds to 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} has practical compression rate 𝒫^i\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{i} that may differ from 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}. However, in practice, we find that {𝒫^i}i=1N\{\hat{\mathcal{P}}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} are extremely close to {𝒫i}i=1N\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, as shown in Figure 2.

The overall process of subnetwork construction is shown in Algorithm 1. It is worth noting that in our construction, the smaller subnetworks are part of the larger ones, which naturally mitigates the interference between them.

5. Model Training

With constructed subnetworks as in Section 4, we are ready to train them in one-shot manner. The target of our OFA compression training is to optimize all supported subnetworks, rendering their performance commensurate with that achieved by separate training. We propose training them by the score matching loss (3) as the original DPM. Ideally, in each update step, we randomly sample a retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, and update the parameters of the corresponding subnetwork under 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} 44 4 Please note that the subnetworks have shared weights and subnetworks are constructed by parameters masks during training, so that the memory overhead will not exceed the standard training process.. Next, we denote the corresponding parameters of 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} as 𝜽𝒫i\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}_{i}}.

It is worth noting that the parameters of all subnetworks are initialized from a pre-trained DPM, thus intuitively, a larger 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} leads to a faster convergence rate of its corresponding subnetwork 𝜽𝒫i\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}_{i}}55 5 The convergence rate of subnetworks are in Appendix C. Consequently, to improve training efficiency, we can balance the convergence progress of subnetwork optimization. We propose to minimize the following reweighting loss in OFA training:

(6) min𝜽⁡𝔼𝒫∈{𝒫i}​[ℒ𝜽𝒫]=∑i=1Nw𝒫i​ℒ𝜽𝒫i,\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{P}\in\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}}}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{N}w_{\mathcal{P}_{i}}\mathcal{L}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}_{i}}},

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} is a discrete distribution over {𝒫i}i=1N\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, and w𝒫iw_{\mathcal{P}_{i}} is the probability of 𝒫\mathcal{P} takes value of 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}. As mentioned above, since a larger 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} corresponds to a faster convergence rate, we propose to make w𝒫iw_{\mathcal{P}_{i}} decrease with 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}. Concretely, we make w𝒫iw_{\mathcal{P}_{i}} linearly descend with ii, and make w𝒫1=m​w𝒫Nw_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}=mw_{\mathcal{P}_{N}} 66 6 These w𝒫iw_{\mathcal{P}_{i}} are normalized with ∑iw𝒫i=1\sum_{i}w_{\mathcal{P}_{i}}=1. for a constant mm (e.g., m=3m=3).

The reweighting strategy is similarly appeared in the existing literature of OFA training. For example, (Yu and Huang, 2019) proposed a sandwich strategy whereas w𝒫1=w𝒫N=0.25w_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}=w_{\mathcal{P}_{N}}=0.25, and the other w𝒫iw_{\mathcal{P}_{i}} are the same constant. However, the strategy is proposed to be applied under training from scratch, and is suboptimal for OFA compression: assigning 25% weights respectively on 𝜽𝒫1\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} and 𝜽𝒫N\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}_{N}} leads to overfitted 𝜽𝒫N\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathcal{P}_{N}} and underfitted other subnetworks. Section 6.3 explores the training strategy and verifies that our proposed strategy performs better.

6. Experiments

6.1. Experimental Setup

Models.

Our experiments are conducted on three representative diffusion models covering different architectures and generation tasks: Elucidating Diffusion Models (EDM) (Karras et al., 2022) based on the standard U-Net architecture, U-ViT (Bao et al., 2023) utilizing the transformer architecture, and Stable Diffusion (SD) (Rombach et al., 2022) for the text-to-image generation task.

Datasets.

To evaluate U-Net-based architectures, we conduct experiments on CIFAR10 32×3232\times 32 (Krizhevsky, 2009), FFHQ 64×6464\times 64 (Karras et al., 2019), and AFHQv2 64×6464\times 64 (Choi et al., 2020) for unconditional generation, alongside ImageNet 64×6464\times 64 (Deng et al., 2009) for class-conditional tasks. For transformer-based architectures, we employ CIFAR10 32×3232\times 32 and CelebA 64×6464\times 64 (Liu et al., 2015). Furthermore, text-to-image generation is evaluated on MS-COCO 2014 (Lin et al., 2014), generating 512×512512\times 512 images from validation captions.

Evaluation.

We use Frechet Inception Distance (FID) score (Heusel et al., 2017) to evaluate the quality of generation. Unless otherwise specified, 50K images are sampled to evaluate the FID score. We also present both the parameter retention rates 𝒫\mathcal{P} and MACs (Multiply-Accumulate operations) of the corresponding subnetworks, where the MACs are measured under one number of function evaluation (NFE=1) with batch size of 1.

Implementation Details.

During OFA training, we construct the search space at the layer level. Specially, different layers can independently choose from a predefined set of discrete retention rates (i.e., 4 candidates). Although this design induces a large combinatorial space of subnetworks, many configurations lead to the same overall parameter count. To calculate importance scores, we sample 1024 pairs (𝒙0,t)(\boldsymbol{x}_{0},t) from training datasets. Our models are mainly U-Net and ViT.

  1. (1)

    For U-Net, our approach is based on EDM (Karras et al., 2022) and Stable-Diffusion v1.5 (Rombach et al., 2022) (Text-to-Image generation). The parameters of our subnetworks are adopted from the pre-trained backbones. After removing the duplicated subnetworks in same size, we obtain 28 unique overall parameter retention rates {𝒫i}i=128\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{28}, covering the range from 0.25 to 1.0. Our method applied to U-Net refers to Figure 6 in Appendix.

  2. (2)

    For transformer-based architectures (ViT), we use U-ViT (Bao et al., 2023), which has 19 {𝒫i}i=119\{\mathcal{P}_{i}\}_{i=1}^{19} sizes of subnetworks after removing duplications, ranging from 0.25 to 1.0. The application to U-ViT refers to Figure 1.

More details of hyperparameters are shown in Appendix B.

6.2. Main Results

Table 1 shows the results of subnetworks derived from our OFA diffusion compression framework. Due to space limits, we show the results of 7 subnetworks here77 7 We visualize some of the performances of all subnetworks extracted from our OFA model in Figure 3.. In Table 1, we compare our method with a competitive baseline, Separate Compression, which compresses subnetworks as in (Fang et al., 2023), with specific parameter retention rates 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} separately. In this regime, the compressed networks do not interfere with each other, while the training overhead increases linearly with the number of models. Besides, we also consider another baseline: the naive implementation of OFA framework as in  (Cai et al., 2020).

As shown in Table 1, our OFA network achieves comparable or even better performance (e.g., averaged FID with 3.05 vs. 3.32 on AFHQv2) with the separate compression baseline across various 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, while enjoying a significant reduction in training overhead (e.g., N×200N\times 200K iterations vs. 200K iterations). Moreover, our approach also significantly improves the naive implementation of OFA training (Cai et al., 2020) for DPMs. In addition, with a slight further fine-tuning, subnetworks extracted from our OFA networks outperform the baselines on most retention rates and still have significantly fewer training computations. Notably, in a smaller retention rate regime (𝒫i<0.5\mathcal{P}_{i}<0.5), our OFA approach beats separate compression by a large margin, suggesting that our method is more suitable in deployment scenarios with limited computational resources. Furthermore, due to the weight-sharing property, our OFA network has less disk storage than the separate compression baseline (e.g., 213M vs. 3578M on CIFAR10). Interestingly, unlike other architectures, OFA compressed networks for Stable Diffusion already achieve highly competitive performance without fine-tuning. Moreover, further fine-tuning does not lead to any additional improvements, which we conjecture is primarily caused by overfitting (Ruiz et al., 2023; Han et al., 2023).

In summary, our OFA diffusion compression framework is able to produce a wide range of compressed subnetworks with competitive performance in a computationally cheap one-shot manner, which helps us to better explore performance-efficiency trade-offs in practical deployment scenarios. The comparison of generated images by these subnetworks are in Appendix F.

Latency Reduction.

We further measure the practical latency of subnetworks under various 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} on both GPU and CPU devices. The results are evaluated on a NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU and an Intel Xeon Gold 6151 CPU, respectively. As shown in Figure 4, we observe that the subnetworks extracted from the OFA network indeed accelerate the original model. This consistent acceleration is observed on both the traditional U-Net (Figure 4a) and the U-ViT architecture (Figure 4b). We find that the retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i} is not exactly the inverse of the actual latency reduction ratio (e.g., 25%25\% vs. 2.4×2.4\times), which also appears in previous channel pruning work (Xia et al., 2022; Tao et al., 2023; Fang et al., 2023). This is because the computation of layer is conducted in parallel, so that reducing the channel width of layers does not linearly decrease the latency. In fact, compressing depth linearly reduce latency, but significantly sacrifices performance (Xia et al., 2022). On the other hand, reducing the width by pruning channels as ours can save memory footprint in the layer-by-layer inference setting (Hou et al., 2021). Thus, considering all of these, we suggest pruning channels as ours in practice.

6.3. Ablation Study

Next, we conduct a series of ablation studies to explore the effectiveness of key components in our OFA diffusion compression framework. For efficiency, we ablate on unconditional generation datasets.

Effects of Subnetworks Construction

As described in Section 4, for each parameter retention rate 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, we specify a target subnetwork constructed based on importance scores of channels in the DPM. We explore the effectiveness of the construction approach Algorithm 1 we devised. First, to investigate the impact of reducing the candidate space in OFA training, we compare our approach with a method adopted in the existing literature (Cai et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2021), Random Architecture, which randomly constructs a subnetwork in each iteration. For each 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, unlike specifying one subnetwork as ours, the Random Architecture has plenty of candidate architectures and requires a post-training search stage to find the optimal candidate88 8 For a fair comparison, we also incorporate the search stage in implementing the Random Architecture ablation, but note that the post-training search also introduce more computation overhead..

Recall that in our approach, the importance scores are defined by the corresponding sensitivity metric (4). We compare our approach with alternative strategies, where channel importance scores are randomly assigned (Random Importance) or calculated according to the L1L_{1} norm of channel weight (Magnitude Importance) (Han et al., 2016), which widely used in previous OFA work on classification task or GANs. For a fair comparison, all variants employ the same training and evaluation settings. Figure 3 shows the performance of our OFA-Diffusion Compression with other ablations. As can be seen:

  1. (1)

    Random Architecture has the worst performance compared with the other methods, demonstrating that reducing the number of useless subnetworks can significantly improve the OFA training.

  2. (2)

    Our approach consistently achieves better averaged FID scores over Random Importance and Magnitude Importance on all datasets, suggesting that our sensitivity-based importance score constructs better subnetworks.

Effects of Reweighting Strategy

Next, we investigate the effect of our reweighting training strategy. Concretely, we compare our linear reweighting strategy clarified in Section 4.2 with ablations: uniform weights on all subnetworks (Uniform) and Sandwich strategy (Sandwich) proposed in (Yu and Huang, 2019): w𝒫1=w𝒫N=0.25w_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}=w_{\mathcal{P}_{N}}=0.25, and other w𝒫iw_{\mathcal{P}_{i}} are the same constant.

The comparison results conducted under U-Net are shown in Table 3. As can be seen, the uniform strategy performs the worst, especially at 0.25×0.25\times, which illustrates the slow convergence of smaller subnetworks during OFA training. More details to the convergence rate of subnetworks in varied sizes refer to Appendix C. In contrast, our reweighting strategy consistently outperforms the Uniform and Sandwich baselines across at almost rates over all datasets, showing that our strategy balances the optimization of subnetworks.

Furthermore, we vary the reweighting ratio between w𝒫1w_{\mathcal{P}_{1}} and w𝒫Nw_{\mathcal{P}_{N}} in our reweighting strategy. The results are shown in Figure 5, where m→1.0m\to 1.0 means w𝒫1=m​w𝒫Nw_{\mathcal{P}_{1}}=mw_{\mathcal{P}_{N}}. When the ratio mm is 3.0 (3.0→1.03.0\to 1.0), the averaged performance is better than the others.

6.4. Discussion

Update Importance during Training.

In Section 4.1, we obtain the importance scores of the channels based on the pre-trained model and fix them in the whole training. We also explore updating the importance score during OFA training to construct subnetworks.

Compute Importance for Different Time.

As the DPMs can be recognized as multitask learning under different time steps tt (Balaji et al., 2022), we also explore calculating the importance score of channels for different tt. That is, for the target 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, the different subnetworks are extracted from the OFA network, which varied with tt.

Unfortunately, compared to the methods in Algorithm 1, both variants obtain worse results. We speculate that these variants implicitly increase the number of candidate subnetworks and may introduce noise in optimization, both of which can slow down the convergence of OFA training. More details refer to the Appendix E.

7. Conclusion

In this work, we propose a novel compression framework for DPMs: the once-for-all (OFA) Diffusion Compression framework, which yields subnetworks of various computational configurations and can flexibly adapt to different hardware and user latency requirements. To alleviate interference between subnetworks, we propose to construct subnetworks based on parameter importance, which identifies and shares important channels among subnetworks and allocates more parameters to more important layers. Furthermore, we propose a reweighting strategy in the training to balance the optimization processes for subnetworks of different sizes. Experimental results on varied architectures show that for the same parameter size, the subnetworks compressed by our OFA framework not only consistently outperform the other OFA baselines but also achieve comparable or even better performance than separate compression, while enjoying a large reduction in training overhead. Since our OFA-Diffusion Compression framework can reduce carbon emissions and is more environmentally friendly, we hope that the framework will facilitate the deployment of diffusion models on a variety of resource-constrained devices for real-life applications.

As illustrated in Fig. 6, we present the overall pipeline of our OFA-Diffusion compression framework built upon the U-Net architecture.

Appendix B Hyperparameters

We adopt the unconditional EDM (Karras et al., 2022) VP model to initialize our OFA diffusion network in the CIFAR1099 9 https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/edm/pretrained/edm-cifar10-32x32-uncond-vp.pkl, FFHQ1010 10 https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/edm/pretrained/edm-ffhq-64x64-uncond-vp.pkl, and AFHQv21111 11 https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/edm/pretrained/edm-afhqv2-64x64-uncond-vp.pkl experiments. Regarding the ImageNet dataset, we use the ADM architecture (Dhariwal and Nichol, 2021) with the EDM precondition1212 12 https://nvlabs-fi-cdn.nvidia.com/edm/pretrained/edm-imagenet-64x64-cond-adm.pkl. For U-ViT, we use the pretrained U-ViT-S/2 model on CIFAR101313 13 https://drive.google.com/file/d/1yoYyuzR_hQYWU0mkTj659tMTnoCWCMv-/view and the U-ViT-S/4 model on CelebA 64×6464\times 641414 14 https://drive.google.com/file/d/13YpbRtlqF1HDBNLNRlKxLTbKbKeLE06C/view provided by Bao et al. (Bao et al., 2023). For Stable Diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022), we use the pretrained SD v1.51515 15 https://huggingface.co/runwayml/stable-diffusion-v1-5 released by RunwayML.

For optimization, we strictly adhere to the default settings of the respective official training scripts to ensure fair comparisons. Specifically, we employ Adam (Kingma and Ba, 2015) for the EDM architecture, and AdamW (Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019) for both U-ViT and Stable Diffusion, preserving their original β\beta configurations. Furthermore, to stabilize the generation quality, we consistently maintain an exponential moving average (EMA) of the network weights.

Detailed hyperparameters are shown in Table 4.

Appendix C The Convergence of Different-Sized Subnetworks

In this section, we show the convergence of subnetworks with different retention rates 𝒫\mathcal{P} for the U-Net architecture on the CIFAR10 32×3232\times 32 dataset. The subnetworks in the OFA-Diffusion Compression framework are initialized from the pre-trained diffusion model. Intuitively, larger subnetworks have more capacity, leading to faster convergence, while smaller ones converge more slowly. We report the ratio of the minimum value of FID during training to the FID at different iterations in Figure 7. We observe that the largest subnetwork (𝒫=0.75\mathcal{P}=0.75) has the fastest convergence, while the smallest subnetwork (𝒫=0.25\mathcal{P}=0.25) has the slowest convergence.

Appendix D Visualization of Layer Importance

In this section, we attempt to visualize the varying importance of layers (calculated as in Section 4.2) in the diffusion model. In Figure 8, we visualize layer importance in the 8×88\times 8 resolution block of the pre-trained EDM (Karras et al., 2022) on CIFAR10 32×3232\times 32 and FFHQ 64×6464\times 64. We also present the sensitivity of layers, which is the FID increase (denoting the performance drop) after removing the corresponding layer. A significant decrease in performance indicates the important role of that layer in the DPM (Kim et al., 2023).

From Fig. 8, we can observe that the importance of layers is consistent with their sensitivity. We find that the innermost layers (the 4th layer of the encoder and the 1st layer of the decoder) have the least importance.

Appendix E Discussions on Importance Scores

As clarified in Section 6.4, channel importance scores can (a) be updated during training or (b) be calculated at different times tt. We experiment with both variants in subnetwork construction:

  1. (1)

    For variant (a), we update the importance scores of channels after every epoch of training, where the importance scores are computed with the sensitivity metric, the same as in (4).

  2. (2)

    Since diffusion training can be viewed as multitask learning over different time steps tt (Balaji et al., 2022), the importance scores can be varied over different tt. Instead of computing importance scores over the whole time interval in EDM (t∈[σ−1​(0.002),σ−1​(80.0)]t\in[\sigma^{-1}(0.002),\allowbreak\sigma^{-1}(80.0)]1616 16 σ−1\sigma^{-1} denotes the inversion function of σ\sigma.), the variant (b) splits the time into 3 intervals: t1∈[σ−1​(0.002),σ−1​(0.1)]t_{1}\in[\sigma^{-1}(0.002),\allowbreak\sigma^{-1}(0.1)], t2∈[σ−1​(0.1),σ−1​(1.0)]t_{2}\in[\sigma^{-1}(0.1),\allowbreak\sigma^{-1}(1.0)], and t3∈[σ−1​(1.0),σ−1​(80.0)]t_{3}\in[\sigma^{-1}(1.0),\allowbreak\sigma^{-1}(80.0)]. For each target 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, the variant (b) constructs three different subnetworks and computes their importance scores according to their corresponding tt. During the sampling process under a specific 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, we use one of the three corresponding models, depending on the time tt.

We compare the above two variants (a) and (b) with the construction approach in Section 4 on CIFAR10 32×3232\times 32. For simplicity, OFA networks are targeted at 4 parameter retention rates 𝒫i∈[0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0]\mathcal{P}_{i}\in\left[0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\right] and trained for 100100K iterations. The results are shown in Table 5.

As can be seen, compared with our method in Algorithm 1, both variants obtain worse results. Thus, we speculate that the two variants are not wise choices in practice. We speculate that these variants implicitly increase the number of candidate subnetworks and may introduce noise in OFA network optimization, both of which can slow down the convergence of training.

Appendix F Samples of Different Subnetworks

In this section, we provide random samples from subnetworks trained by different approaches under various 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}, as shown in Figures 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15. We observe that the subnetworks extracted from our OFA network can generate high-quality samples with clear semantics.
